# How bacteria are built and get energy

> *A stain turns some bacteria purple and others pink, and some bacteria die in air while others
> grow best in it. Both differences follow from how a bacterium is built and how it makes energy.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Compare a bacterium with a human cell, and relate each difference to selective toxicity.
- Describe the four envelope designs, and explain how the Gram stain separates Gram-positive from
  Gram-negative bacteria.
- Explain what capsules, pili, flagella, biofilms and spores do for a bacterium and for the host.
- Distinguish aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation.
- Place a bacterium in an oxygen group from its metabolism, and predict where in the body it can
  live.
- Calculate the growth of a population from its doubling time.
:::

## The bacterial cell {#sec-bact-cell}

### A bacterium and a human cell {#sec-bact-glance}

Try two questions before reading on.

<div data-island="quiz" data-src="/quizzes/bacteria-warmup.quiz.yml"></div>

A bacterium is a prokaryote, and a typical bacterium is about the size of one human mitochondrion
(see the size ladder in [*The microbial world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-scale)). It differs
from a human cell in its nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, wall and extra DNA. Each difference is a
possible basis for **selective toxicity**: harming the microbe without harming the host, the
principle behind most antimicrobial drugs.

| Feature | Human cells | A bacterium | Why the difference matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | DNA inside a nuclear envelope | No nucleus; one circular chromosome lies free in the cytoplasm | Transcription and translation happen together (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-copy)) |
| Mitochondria | Electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane | No mitochondria; electron transport chain in the cell membrane | Bacterial respiration happens at the cell surface |
| Ribosomes | 80S | 70S, smaller and built differently | A target human cytoplasmic ribosomes do not share |
| Cell wall | None | Usually a peptidoglycan wall outside the membrane | A structure human cells lack entirely |
| Extra DNA | Mitochondrial DNA only | Often small circles of DNA called plasmids | Plasmids carry genes between bacteria |

::: {.callout-important}
## Do bacteria have mitochondria?
Students starting microbiology often credit prokaryotes with mitochondria
[@briggs2017misconceptions]. The slip is understandable, because bacteria do respire, but they
respire on their own cell membrane. The likeness runs the other way: mitochondria descend from
bacteria that came to live inside an ancestral cell, which is why mitochondria have their own
circular DNA and bacterial-type ribosomes.
:::

### The cell envelope {#sec-bact-envelope}

A bacterium's **cell envelope** is its cell membrane and every layer outside it. The envelope has
three functions:

- it holds the cell together;
- it controls what enters and leaves;
- it carries most of the molecules the host immune system recognises.

The cytoplasm of a bacterium is full of dissolved molecules, so water enters by osmosis, and without
support the cell would swell and burst (**osmotic lysis**). The support comes from **peptidoglycan**, a
mesh of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides that surrounds the whole cell like a string bag
[@silhavy2010envelope].

Most bacteria build their envelope in one of two ways. In **Gram-positive** bacteria, a thick
peptidoglycan wall, many layers deep, lies directly outside the cell membrane, and there is no outer
membrane. In **Gram-negative** bacteria, a thin layer of peptidoglycan lies between the cell membrane
and a second, **outer membrane**, whose outer face is made of **lipopolysaccharide (LPS)**.

The Gram stain, devised by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, reads this difference in a few minutes, and
laboratories still use it to sort most bacteria. Step through it below, and predict which step
separates the two groups before it is revealed.

<div data-island="gram-stain" data-src="/diagrams/gram-stain.yml"></div>

Two kinds of bacteria fit neither design. *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* has a wall packed with waxy
**mycolic acids**. Gram's dyes barely penetrate it, so mycobacteria are detected with the
**acid-fast stain**, in which the waxy wall keeps a red dye even when washed with acid-alcohol. At the
other extreme, *Mycoplasma* has no wall at all. It does not show up on a Gram stain, and drugs aimed
at the wall have nothing to act on.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Envelope designs]{.tree-title}

- Bacterial envelopes
  - With a wall
    - Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane (*Staphylococcus aureus*)
    - Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan under an outer membrane with LPS (*Escherichia coli*)
    - Acid-fast: a wall packed with waxy mycolic acids (*M. tuberculosis*)
  - With no wall (*Mycoplasma*)
:::

The structure of the envelope has three consequences for the host:

- Lipid A, the lipid portion of LPS, binds immune receptors and drives strong inflammation: the
  fever and the dilated, leaky vessels described in general pathology [@raetz2002lps]. Because this
  toxic molecule is part of the bacterial cell and is not secreted, LPS is also called **endotoxin**.
- The outer membrane keeps out many molecules, including some drugs, that reach a Gram-positive
  cell's membrane easily.
- Peptidoglycan has no counterpart in human cells, so drugs that block its construction harm
  bacteria and spare the host.

### Shape and arrangement {#sec-bact-shape}

Bacteria come in three basic shapes: **cocci** (spheres), **bacilli** (rods), and curved or spiral
forms. Arrangement reflects how the cell divides. Cocci that divide in one plane stay attached in
chains, as streptococci do; cocci that divide in several planes form clusters, as staphylococci do.
Find the feature that separates the two in the activity below before the explanation appears.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-staph-strep.yml"></div>

### Capsules, appendages, biofilms and spores {#sec-bact-extras}

Many bacteria carry structures beyond the envelope. Each solves a problem for the bacterium and has a
consequence for the host.

| Structure | What it is | What it does for the bacterium | Why it matters to the host |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capsule | A slimy outer layer, usually polysaccharide | Hides the cell surface; resists drying | Phagocytes find it hard to engulf ([*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-steps)) |
| Pili (fimbriae) | Short, hair-like protein fibres | Attach the cell to surfaces, including host cells | Attachment is often the first step of colonisation |
| Flagella | Long, rotating protein filaments | Swimming towards nutrients | Let bacteria move into new sites |
| Biofilm | A community of cells in a shared slime matrix | Shelter from drying, predators and chemicals | Forms on teeth and on medical devices such as catheters |
| Endospore | A dormant, dehydrated cell inside protective coats | Survives starvation, heat and chemicals for years | Hard to kill with routine heat or disinfectants |

Spores are made by a few groups of Gram-positive rods, notably *Bacillus* and *Clostridium*. When
nutrients run out, the cell builds a spore inside itself: a copy of its DNA wrapped in a dehydrated
core and several protective coats [@setlow2014spores]. When conditions improve, the spore germinates
back into a growing cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Predict: will boiling or an alcohol hand rub kill spores? (Click to check)
Mostly not. Many spores survive boiling at 100 °C, and alcohol hand rubs do not kill them
[@setlow2014spores]. Reliable killing needs pressurised steam at 121 °C, as in an autoclave (see
[*Detecting and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-control) for instruments and
hand hygiene).
:::

## Energy and oxygen {#sec-bact-metabolism}

### Getting energy {#sec-bact-energy}

Bacteria make ATP with the same chemistry as human cells, but with more options. Human cells break
down glucose by glycolysis and pass the electrons down an electron transport chain to oxygen. Many
bacteria use the same two stages, but oxygen need not be the final electron acceptor.

| Strategy | What happens | Final electron acceptor | ATP per glucose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aerobic respiration | Glycolysis, then an electron transport chain in the cell membrane | Oxygen | High, similar to human cells |
| Anaerobic respiration | The same, without oxygen | Another molecule, such as nitrate or sulfate | Lower |
| Fermentation | Glycolysis only; pyruvate is converted to products such as lactate or ethanol | An organic molecule made from glucose, such as pyruvate; no electron transport chain | Low, about 2 |

Human skeletal muscle ferments glucose to lactate during a sprint, when oxygen supply cannot keep up.
Some bacteria live this way all the time.

### The oxygen spectrum {#sec-bact-oxygen}

Oxygen is the most effective electron acceptor available, but it is also chemically dangerous.
Partly reduced oxygen forms **reactive oxygen species**, such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide,
which damage proteins and DNA. We met these in cell biology as by-products of human mitochondria.

Bacteria range from those that cannot grow without oxygen to those that oxygen kills:

::: {.spectrum}
[Relationship with oxygen]{.tree-title}

- *M. tuberculosis*: makes ATP only with oxygen
- *E. coli*: respires with oxygen, ferments without it
- *Bacteroides fragilis*: killed by oxygen

[Obligate aerobe]{.spectrum-end} [Obligate anaerobe]{.spectrum-end}
:::

Two questions place a bacterium along this range: can the organism use oxygen to make ATP, and is it
harmed by oxygen at atmospheric levels? The **microaerophiles**, which need a little oxygen but are
harmed by air, form a fifth group alongside the four that the two questions produce.

| Group | Uses oxygen to make ATP? | Harmed by normal air? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Obligate aerobe | Yes, and has no alternative | No | *M. tuberculosis* |
| Facultative anaerobe | Yes, when oxygen is present; ferments otherwise | No | *E. coli*, *S. aureus* |
| Microaerophile | Yes, but only at low oxygen levels | Yes, at atmospheric levels | *Helicobacter pylori*, a stomach bacterium ([*The microbial world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-case)) |
| Aerotolerant anaerobe | No; ferments only | No; its enzymes are not inactivated by oxygen | *Streptococcus pyogenes* |
| Obligate anaerobe | No | Yes | *B. fragilis* |

From how an organism handles energy and oxygen, we can work out where it will grow. Place each
organism below, described only by its metabolism; its name appears after each choice.

<div data-island="oxygen-tube" data-src="/diagrams/oxygen-tube.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## Do anaerobes die because they lack catalase and superoxide dismutase?
Older textbooks explain oxygen toxicity this way, extrapolating from an observation made in the
1970s. Many anaerobes do carry these protective enzymes; *B. fragilis*, for example, makes both.
Oxygen kills anaerobes by damaging the machinery they depend on: central enzymes built around exposed
iron–sulfur clusters or radical chemistry, which oxygen and reactive oxygen species inactivate
directly [@lu2021anaerobes].
:::

### Oxygen in the body {#sec-bact-body}

The human body has oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor sites:

- Skin and airways are exposed to air.
- The colon contains almost no oxygen, and anaerobes there outnumber facultative bacteria many times
  over.
- Oxygen-poor sites also appear when tissue loses its blood supply: **ischaemic** (poorly perfused)
  and necrotic tissue, and the centre of an abscess, contain little oxygen and suit anaerobes.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-ecoli-bacteroides.yml"></div>

## Growth {#sec-bact-growth}

Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**: the cell copies its chromosome, grows, and splits in two.
The time a population takes to double in number is its **doubling time**. In ideal laboratory
conditions *E. coli* doubles about every 20 minutes, while *M. tuberculosis* takes most of a day.

Starting from $N_0$ cells, after time $t$ with doubling time $g$:

$$ N = N_0 \times 2^{t/g} $$

::: {.example}
One *E. coli* cell doubling every 20 minutes becomes about 17 million cells in 8 hours, which is 24
doublings. *M. tuberculosis* takes weeks to form a visible colony, so its culture also takes weeks.
:::

In a closed container, a population passes through four phases:

::: {.flow}
1. Lag phase
2. Exponential (log) phase
3. Stationary phase
4. Death phase
:::

The balance of division and death changes from phase to phase:

- In the lag phase, cells adjust to new conditions and divide little.
- In the exponential phase, cells double steadily, as in the equation above.
- In the stationary phase, nutrients run low and waste accumulates, so division and death balance.
- In the death phase, more cells die than divide.

Rapidly dividing cells are the most vulnerable to many antimicrobial drugs.

## Describing a bacterium {#sec-bact-describe}

### Two microbe profiles {#sec-bact-profiles}

A microbe profile records five facts about an organism:

- *identity and structure*;
- *lifestyle and niche*;
- *mechanism of harm*;
- *general consequence*;
- a *contrast partner* it is easily confused with.

The first card below has three slots filled in; predict the other two. The second has one.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-s-aureus.yml"></div>

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-b-fragilis.yml"></div>

*S. aureus* and *B. fragilis* both live harmlessly on or in many healthy people
[@kluytmans1997carriage], and both cause harm mainly when they reach a site where they do not belong.
Both tend to cause **pyogenic** (pus-forming) infection and abscesses, and the capsule of *B. fragilis*
actively promotes abscess formation [@tzianabos1993abscess]. They differ in envelope, Gram-positive
against Gram-negative, and in their relationship with oxygen, facultative against obligately
anaerobic.

### The trait toolkit {#sec-bact-toolkit}

Five traits describe any bacterium:

| Trait | The options | What it indicates |
|---|---|---|
| Envelope | Gram-positive, Gram-negative, acid-fast (waxy), no wall | Whether the immune system meets LPS; what can enter the cell; whether drugs aimed at the wall can act |
| Shape and arrangement | Cocci, rods, curved or spiral; clusters, chains, pairs | Clues to identity and to how the cell divides |
| Additional structures | Capsule, pili, flagella, biofilm, spores | How it attaches, moves, hides and survives outside a host |
| Energy and oxygen | Aerobe, facultative, microaerophile, aerotolerant, anaerobe | Where in the body it can live; how a sample must be handled |
| Growth rate | Doubling in minutes, or in about a day | How fast an infection develops; how long culture takes |
